summary: Gives terminology and a model of a typical Network Access Server (NAS), the device that connects dial-up users to a network. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This draws a picture of the machine that answers your dial-up call and lets you into the network, and names its parts.

questions: what is a network access server
how does a nas authenticate users
how does a nas do accounting
subtitle: A reference model for Network Access Servers that authenticate users and manage network access.

tldr.problem: Network Access Servers (NAS) have grown without formal definition or analysis, making it difficult to describe and evaluate NAS service protocols and requirements.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2881 defines the terminology and gives a reference model of a typical NAS, describing its major functional components: authentication, authorization, accounting, and auditing.
tldr.outcome: This informational model provides the foundation for evaluating NAS protocols like RADIUS and Diameter, and guides the design of AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) systems.

today: RFC 2881 remains the foundational reference model for Network Access Servers in the Internet. It has not been obsoleted and continues to guide the design of AAA protocols and NAS implementations for dial-up access, VPNs, and remote access services.

sections.title: What Is a Network Access Server
sections.content:
A Network Access Server (NAS) is the initial entry point to a network for most users seeking network services. It acts as a gateway between end users and network services, making its role crucial to both users and service providers. The RFC establishes a formal model where a NAS has grown organically over the years without being formally defined or analyzed.

The document's purpose is to provide a reference model for evaluating NAS service protocols such as RADIUS and Diameter, and to give a framework for understanding how NAS systems work and what requirements protocols must satisfy.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS is like a bouncer at a club door. The RFC explains how bouncers check who you are, what they let you do, and keep track of everything.

sections.title: NAS Model and Components
sections.content:
The RFC presents a reference model showing a NAS with distinct interfaces and functional components. A NAS has client interfaces where users connect (via modems, tunnels, or other means) and network interfaces that connect to the networks being accessed. The model distinguishes between Dial Access Servers (with modem connections) and Tunnel Servers (with tunneling protocol endpoints like L2TP).

The policy management interface allows per-user service management through a protocol like RADIUS, Diameter, or COPS. The device management interface, typically SNMP, handles the NAS itself rather than user-specific policies. These are separate concerns: the AAA server authorizes user services, while network management configures the NAS as a device.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS has a front door (where users plug in), a back door (to the network), and a control room (where policies about what each user can do are set).

sections.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting
sections.content:
Authentication is where the NAS verifies that a user is who they claim to be, using credentials like passwords, tokens, or certificates. Authorization grants specific types of service to an authenticated user based on their identity and policies—for example, assigning an IP address, setting bandwidth limits, or requiring encryption. Accounting tracks resource consumption (connection time, data transferred) for management, billing, or auditing.

A separate Auditing function tracks the nature of user activity to verify conformance to policies or to investigate security issues. These four functions work together: the NAS authenticates the user, gets authorization from a server, delivers the authorized service, and logs usage for later accounting and auditing.
sections.plainLanguage: First you prove who you are. Then the system says what you can do. Then it counts what you actually used. And finally it checks if everything was okay.

sections.title: Typical NAS Operation
sections.content:
When a user connects to a NAS, a typical sequence follows. First, the NAS detects the call or connection. If it's a PPP connection, the NAS engages link control and authentication negotiation. The NAS then requests authentication from an external AAA server, which may challenge the user or require password changes. Once authentication succeeds, the NAS requests authorization information—what service the user is entitled to and under what restrictions.

The authorized service is then provided. Throughout the session, the NAS collects accounting information about resource usage. At session end, an accounting record is sent to track what was consumed. The RFC notes that calls can be busied out based on caller ID or called number before authentication, and that the NAS may support multiple link aggregation, tunneling, and callback services.
sections.plainLanguage: The sequence is: someone calls the door, the bouncer checks them at the window, the boss approves them, they get in, we keep track while they're inside, and we write down what happened when they leave.

sections.title: NAS Services and Virtual Private Networks
sections.content:
A NAS provides diverse services to users. Common examples include dial-up access, SLIP and PPP network access, asynchronous terminal services (Telnet), callback services, and tunneling to remote servers. The RFC notes that a NAS may sit at the edge of the network as an Edge Server providing dynamic access to both private and public networks.

Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) are a significant NAS function. A NAS may build compulsory tunnels for security or support voluntary tunneling endpoints. The RFC also covers roaming scenarios where a NAS operator grants access to users from other service providers. Resource management is dynamic—the NAS allocates IP addresses, controls bandwidth, applies packet filters, and enforces Quality of Service (QoS) policies, all based on per-user authorization from the AAA server.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAS can let people dial in, tunnel to a remote office, share bandwidth fairly, and work with other networks that trust each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several security concerns for NAS systems. The NAS must provide robust authentication appropriate to network policies and authenticate itself to users. It should protect authentication information from snooping and defend against replay and man-in-the-middle attacks. The NAS must prevent unauthorized hosts from probing or guessing authentication information or gaining unauthorized services.

Since a NAS may be shared among multiple administrative entities (such as in roaming scenarios), authentication may occur via back-end proxy, referral, or brokering processes. The NAS itself may operate as a secure device with secure management, IP Security, and participation in public key infrastructure. Finally, the NAS should protect the network from illegal packets sourced by connecting users through filtering and anti-spoofing controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Secrets must stay secret, bad guys must not get in, and things the NAS passes should be checked to make sure they're really from who they claim to be from.
